objectives: Name a major key by counting the sharps or flats in its signature
A major has three sharps; B♭ major has two flats and E♭ major three
Sharps and flats each arrive in a fixed order, so the count alone names the key

concept.title: Counting the signature
concept.body: Grade 1 gave you two sharp keys and one flat key. Three more follow the same rule. A major has three sharps: F♯, C♯ and G♯. B♭ major has two flats, B♭ and E♭; E♭ major has three, adding A♭. The sharps always arrive in the order F♯ C♯ G♯ and the flats as B♭ E♭ A♭, never in a different order and never skipping one, so the count alone names the key. Read the signature left to right, count what you see, and stop. Notice that the second flat, E♭, is also the name of the key that has three of them.

teach.smartTip: Count them: three sharps is A major; two flats is B♭ major, three flats is E♭ major.
teach.didYouKnow: Flats are written in the order B, E, A, D, G, C, F — exactly the sharp order (F, C, G, D, A, E, B) reversed.

objectives: The three relative pairs: A minor with C major, E minor with G major, D minor with F major
A key and its relative minor or major always share the same key signature
How to count a minor 3rd down from a major tonic to find its relative minor

concept.title: Grade 2 relative minor keys
concept.body: Every major key has a relative minor that shares its key signature. C major and A minor both have no sharps or flats; G major and E minor both have one sharp, F♯; F major and D minor both have one flat, B♭. The relative minor's tonic sits a minor 3rd below its major partner's.

teach.smartTip: Count three semitones — a minor 3rd — down from the major tonic and you'll land on the relative minor, two letter-names lower: C down to A, G down to E, F down to D.
teach.didYouKnow: A relative major and minor share every note in their scale, yet sound completely different — because their home note, the tonic, is different.

objectives: Harmonic minor is the natural minor with the 7th note raised
Where the scale's semitones fall — three of them, plus the augmented 2nd between the 6th and 7th notes
The raised 7ths for A, E and D minor: G♯, D♯ and C♯

concept.title: Grade 2 harmonic minor
concept.body: Harmonic minor is built from the natural (key-signature) minor scale with one change: the 7th note is raised a semitone. That raised 7th creates an augmented 2nd — a gap of three semitones — between the 6th and 7th notes, which is what gives harmonic minor its distinctive sound. A minor's raised 7th is G♯, E minor's is D♯, and D minor's is C♯.

teach.smartTip: The 7th is raised with an accidental, written note by note — it is never written in the key signature.
teach.didYouKnow: The augmented-2nd gap between the 6th and 7th notes is what gives harmonic minor its distinctive, almost exotic sound.

objectives: Name any note of a major scale by its degree number
The keynote is the 1st degree, so the count starts at one, not zero
The rule is the same in A, B♭ and E♭

concept.title: Counting from the keynote
concept.body: The rule you learned at Grade 1 does not change with the key. The keynote is the 1st degree and the numbers count up the letter names from it. What changes is which notes those numbers land on. In B♭ major the 1st degree is B♭, the 2nd is C, the 3rd is D. In A major the 1st is A and the 3rd is C♯. Read the key signature first, decide the keynote, then count. Minor keys number the same way from their own keynote.

teach.smartTip: Read the key signature, find the keynote, then count letter names up from it.
teach.didYouKnow: This is why a singer can be told 'you are flat on the 3rd' without anyone naming a note. The degree number is the same instruction in every key.

lessons.title: Tonic triads in the new keys

objectives: Build the tonic triad of a major key in root position
The tonic triad is the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked
Root position means the keynote is the lowest note

concept.title: Three notes that fix the key
concept.body: The tonic triad is still the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked, whatever the key. In B♭ major that gives B♭, D and F; in E♭ major, E♭, G and B♭. The key signature supplies any flat or sharp, so you rarely need to write an accidental — build the triad from the letter names and let the signature do the rest. A minor key's tonic triad works the same way from its own keynote.

teach.smartTip: Keynote, skip, skip. The key signature supplies the accidentals; you supply the letters.
teach.didYouKnow: Because the pattern is always 1-3-5, a player can find the tonic triad of an unfamiliar key without knowing a single one of its notes by name.

objectives: Read a time signature whose beat is a minim, not a crotchet
The top number counts beats; the bottom number says which note is the beat
3/8 counts three quavers, and is usually felt as one beat

concept.title: The bottom number chooses the beat
concept.body: Every signature so far had a 4 underneath, so the beat was a crotchet. The bottom number is what picks the beat, and 2 means a minim. So 3/2 is three minim beats in a bar, counted exactly like 3/4 but written in longer notes. 4/2 is four. The music does not go slower — the note values are simply larger, which is why 2/2 is often written as a C with a line through it and called cut time. 8 underneath means the beat is a quaver: 3/8 holds three of them, and at speed you feel the whole bar as one.

teach.smartTip: Read the bottom number first. It tells you what to count; the top number tells you how many.
teach.didYouKnow: The C used for 4/4 is not an abbreviation of 'common'. It is a broken circle: medieval scribes drew a full circle for triple time, which they thought perfect, and a broken one for duple.

objectives: A triplet plays three notes in the time of two of the same value
The group fills exactly one beat, whatever the beat is
A rest inside the group still takes up one of its three places

concept.title: Three in the time of two
concept.body: A beat normally splits in two. A triplet splits it in three instead, and the small 3 above the group is what tells you. The three notes together last exactly one beat, so three quavers under a triplet bracket fill a crotchet beat that would otherwise hold two quavers. Whatever the beat is, the rule is the same: three in the time of two. A triplet can also contain a rest. The bracket still covers three places and still fills one beat, but one of those places is silent, so only two notes sound.

teach.smartTip: Count the beat, not the notes. Three triplet quavers take exactly as long as two ordinary ones.
teach.didYouKnow: Playing a triplet against a duplet in the other hand is called a cross-rhythm. Brahms wrote whole movements on it, and pianists still count them out loud.

objectives: Recognise the Grade 2 tempo words and the words that modify a speed
The endings -etto and -ino make a word less extreme, not more
Ritenuto is an immediate change; rallentando is gradual

concept.title: Filling in the speeds
concept.body: Grade 1 gave you a ladder from adagio to allegro. Grade 2 fills in the rungs between and beyond. LARGO and LENTO are slow, GRAVE slower and heavier still; PRESTO is fast and VIVACE is lively. Two endings do a lot of work: -ETTO makes a word gentler, so LARGHETTO is less slow than largo, and ADAGIETTO less slow than adagio. -INO does something similar to andantino. Then there are the words that change a speed rather than set one: MENO MOSSO is less movement, PIÙ MOSSO is more, CON MOTO is with movement, and RITENUTO holds back at once rather than gradually.

teach.smartTip: -etto and -ino soften a word. Larghetto is less slow than largo, not more.
teach.didYouKnow: Ritenuto and rallentando are often confused even by players. Rallentando slows gradually; ritenuto drops the speed immediately, like a handbrake rather than a gentle brake.

objectives: Recognise the Grade 2 words for character and degree
Poco, molto, non troppo and sempre never stand alone
Senza means without; simile means carry on the same way

concept.title: How much, and in what mood
concept.body: Two kinds of word here, and they work together. The first names a mood for a whole passage: ESPRESSIVO expressive, GRAZIOSO graceful, GIOCOSO playful. The second says HOW MUCH of something else — POCO a little, POCO A POCO little by little, MOLTO very, NON TROPPO not too much, SEMPRE always. Those four never appear alone; they attach to another word and adjust it, so allegro non troppo is fast but not too fast, and cresc. poco a poco is a swell that arrives gradually. SENZA means without, and it works the same way: senza rit. is an instruction not to slow down.

teach.smartTip: Poco, molto, non troppo and sempre always modify the word next to them. Read the pair, not the word.
teach.didYouKnow: Non troppo exists because players kept overdoing it. Allegro non troppo is a composer saying 'yes, fast — but I have heard what you do with allegro, and not that fast.'

lessons.title: Marks and signs on the page

objectives: Recognise the Grade 2 articulation marks and navigation signs
Tenuto, fortepiano and sforzando each shape a single note
Dal segno, al fine and 8va tell you where to go, not how to play

concept.title: Shaping a note, and finding your way
concept.body: These do two jobs. Three of them shape a single note: TENUTO holds it for its full value, FORTEPIANO (fp) attacks it loudly then drops instantly to quiet, and SFORZANDO (sf) forces it out. The rest are navigation. DAL SEGNO (D.S.) sends you back to the sign, AL FINE says play on to the word 'fine', and 8VA moves a passage an octave from where it is written. SIMILE says carry on in the same way, so a pattern already established does not have to be re-marked on every note.

teach.smartTip: fp is one instruction, not two: loud then immediately quiet, on the same note.
teach.didYouKnow: Writing 8va above a passage saves a copyist from drawing five ledger lines on every note. It survived into print because it is genuinely easier to read.
